inPerson.q: Can I accept Monero in person at a shop or market stall?
inPerson.p1: Yes. Create a terminal in the dashboard and open its link on a tablet or phone at your till. Type the amount, the customer scans the QR code with their wallet, and the screen shows “Payment seen” once the payment reaches the network, usually within seconds. Funds go directly to your wallet.
inPerson.p2: With zero confirmations the payment is not yet in a block and could in rare cases fail to confirm; require confirmations for larger amounts. Each sale uses one of your invoice addresses, and unpaid or cancelled sales hold theirs for three days.

donations.q: Can I use payment links to accept Monero donations?
donations.p1: Yes. Create a payment link to your own wallet, give it a title such as “Support my project”, choose Customer enters the amount, and set Button text to “Donate with Monero”. Share its reusable URL or copy the HTML button to your website. Each successful submission creates a separate XMR invoice; funds go directly to your wallet.
donations.p2: Donors enter an amount in XMR or a supported fiat-reference currency; you can set a minimum in XMR. To offer preset amounts instead, create a fixed-amount link for each. Automatic recurring collection is not supported. Existing invoice allowances and address limits apply even when an invoice is never paid.

badge.q: Do you have a “Monero accepted here” badge or sign?
badge.p1: Yes. Dashboard → Payment links has a “Monero accepted here” badge to copy into your website, and each payment link has a printable sign with a QR code for a counter, stall, or donation box. The badge is a plain image with no tracking.

noWoo.q: Can I add a payment button without WooCommerce?
noWoo.p1: Yes. Configure a fixed XMR amount or a supported fiat-reference amount in Dashboard → Payment links, then copy an HTML button into your website. If your editor removes forms, use the reusable URL. No programming or WooCommerce integration is required.

vsQr.q: How is a reusable payment link different from a wallet QR code?
vsQr.p1: A static wallet QR code does not create a separate invoice for each purchase. A payment button requests a new invoice on submission. Opening the reusable URL first shows a review page; submitting there requests the invoice. The invoice has its own ID and payment status for reconciliation.

repeat.q: Do repeated clicks reuse an invoice or guarantee a new address?
repeat.p1: Separate submissions can create separate invoices; plain HTML has no duplicate-submission recovery. A fresh invoice does not guarantee an address that has never been used: the merchant address pool eventually reuses eligible addresses after its cooldown. Late payments after reuse can still be confused with newer invoices. Check the dashboard allowance and address availability, and contact the merchant before retrying an interrupted creation request.

digital.q: Can payment links deliver digital products such as ebooks?
digital.p1: Yes, with a confirmation message. Each payment link can show its own plain-text message on the invoice page after the required confirmations, such as a download link, a shared license key, or delivery instructions. To sell five ebooks, create five links, each with its own download link. The message is not sent to the browser before confirmation.
digital.p2: Every buyer of a link sees the same message, and files are not hosted by XMR Checkout. For protected or per-buyer downloads, use expiring links or webhooks with the invoice ID. Payment links collect no buyer details.

custodial.p1: No. Payments go directly from the customer to your Monero wallet. XMR Checkout only observes the blockchain to detect payments and update invoice status.

access.q: What wallet access does XMR Checkout require?
access.p1: The maximum permission we ask for is view-only access: your primary address and your private view key. We never request spend keys and we never request signing access.

setup.p1: After signing in, create invoices from the dashboard or API.

email.q: Do you require email or personal information?
email.p1: No. We do not require email or personal information. Your primary address is the identifier for access, paired with your private view key.

cost.p1: Currently, xmrcheckout.com does not charge a service fee. You can also self-host the open source stack if you prefer.
cost.p2: If you find XMR Checkout useful, you can support development with <link>donations</link>.

moveFunds.q: Can XMR Checkout move funds, issue refunds, or reverse payments?
moveFunds.p1: No. XMR Checkout does not sign transactions and cannot move funds on your behalf. It is checkout software: create invoices, detect payments, and relay status via API/webhooks.

receipt.q: How do customers get a receipt?
receipt.p1: Once a payment is confirmed, the payment page links to a receipt the customer can print or save. XMR Checkout does not collect customer email addresses or send email. If you email your customers, include the receipt_url from the invoice.confirmed webhook.

down.q: What happens if XMR Checkout is down when a customer pays?
down.p1: Your wallet can still receive a valid on-chain payment because the payment is customer → merchant wallet. If the service is unavailable, you may temporarily lose invoice status updates until it comes back online.

hosted.q: How does XMR Checkout differ from hosted services (e.g. NOWPayments)?
hosted.p1: The main differences are scope, custody model, and data collection: XMR Checkout is Monero-only and does not require an account or email.
hosted.li1: Monero-only: a focused product without a multi-asset stack.
hosted.li2: No account/email: your primary address is the identifier.
hosted.li3: No custody: payments go directly to your wallet.
hosted.li4: Clear failure modes: downtime can delay status updates, but it does not affect on-chain validity of payments.
hosted.after: If you use a third-party service, review what keys and data it requires, and whether it ever takes custody or intermediates funds.

btcpay.q: How does XMR Checkout differ from BTCPay Server?
btcpay.p1: BTCPay Server is a general-purpose, self-hosted payment server with a primary focus on Bitcoin and optional integrations for other assets (including Monero via a plugin). XMR Checkout is intentionally focused on Monero checkout and a minimal, deterministic core.
btcpay.p2: Some hosted BTCPay deployments may not include the Monero plugin by default. XMR Checkout provides a small compatibility layer so teams can integrate without running a full BTCPay deployment.
btcpay.li1: Monero-first UX: invoice and confirmation language is tailored to Monero.
btcpay.li2: Fewer moving parts: a narrow scope keeps operations and audits simpler.
btcpay.li3: API/webhooks-first: designed to fit into existing order systems.

selfHost.p1: Yes. XMR Checkout is open source, and you can self-host it from the official <github>GitHub repository</github>.
selfHost.p2: Start with <docs>Documentation</docs> or the <guide>self-hosting guide</guide> for setup and integration details.

inPerson.title: Accept Monero in person with a terminal
inPerson.metaDescription: Turn a tablet or phone into a Monero till. Type the amount, show a QR code, and see the payment arrive in seconds, paid directly to your wallet.
inPerson.intro: For cafés, market stalls, meetups, and shops. A terminal is a page on a tablet or phone at your till. Each sale is a normal XMR invoice paid directly to your wallet. The terminal never receives or holds funds.

setup.title: Set up a terminal
setup.step1: Connect your wallet with your primary address and private view key. Never enter a private spend key or recovery seed.
setup.step2: Open Dashboard → Terminals and choose Create terminal. Give it a name such as “Front counter”, and pick a default currency.
setup.step3: The dashboard shows the terminal link and a QR code once. Scan it with the device you will use at the till, or copy the link to it.
setup.step4: On the device, add the page to the home screen for a full-screen till. The device remembers the terminal until you choose Forget this terminal.
setup.p1: To let customers know they can pay with Monero, print the Monero accepted here badge from Dashboard → Payment links and place it by the till. More ways to let people find you

sale.title: Take a payment
sale.step1: Type the amount on the number pad, add an optional note such as “2 coffees”, and tap Charge.
sale.step2: Turn the screen to the customer. They scan the QR code with their Monero wallet and send the payment.
sale.step3: The screen shows Payment seen once the payment reaches the network, usually within 5–20 seconds.
sale.step4: Tap New sale for the next customer. If the customer changes their mind before paying, tap Cancel sale.
sale.p1: Amounts in a fiat currency are converted to XMR at a reference rate when the invoice is created. The rate is informational and no fiat outcome is guaranteed. Every sale appears in your invoice list and CSV export with the terminal name and note.

confirmations.title: Choose confirmations
confirmations.p1: With zero confirmations, which is the default for terminals, the screen shows “Payment seen” as soon as the transaction reaches the network. It is not yet in a block. In rare cases a transaction seen this way never confirms. For small, everyday amounts that risk is usually acceptable.
confirmations.p2: For larger amounts, set one or more confirmations. Each confirmation takes about two minutes. The screen shows progress until the target is reached.

security.title: Keep the link safe
security.p1: The terminal link can only create invoices to your wallet, show their status, and cancel its own unpaid sales. It cannot move funds, change settings, or open your dashboard.
security.p2: If a device is lost, open the terminal in the dashboard and choose Create new link. The old link stops working immediately. You can also disable a terminal at any time.

limits.title: Address capacity
limits.p1: Every invoice uses one of your 199 invoice addresses. After an invoice closes, its address is held for three days so a late payment is never credited to a different customer. Cancelled and unpaid sales hold an address too.
limits.p2: This allows about 66 sales a day on average. The terminal shows a warning when fewer than 20 addresses are free. The dashboard shows when held addresses become available again.

buttons.title: Accept Monero with payment and donation links
buttons.metaDescription: Accept payments or donations directly to your wallet. Share a reusable Monero link or embed an HTML button without programming.
buttons.intro: Accept Monero on an independent website without WooCommerce or an API integration. Use payment links for products, services, or donations to your own wallet. Configure a fixed amount or let the customer enter one in the dashboard, then paste a button into an HTML block or share a reusable link.

1.1: Connect your wallet using your primary address and private view key. Never submit a private spend key or recovery seed. Customer payments go directly to your wallet.
1.2: Open Dashboard → Payment links, then choose Create payment link.
1.3: Enter a title and optional description. For example, use “Digital guide” with a fixed amount of 20 and currency EUR. You can also choose an exact XMR amount, or select Customer enters the amount to let the customer type it (see donations).
1.4: Choose your required confirmations. The form starts with your merchant default; zero accepts detection without waiting for a block confirmation. Optionally add an HTTPS merchant return URL and a <message>confirmation message</message> shown after payment.
1.5: Leave Enable new purchases selected and save. Set Button text to customize the graphic label (up to 32 characters). The default is “Buy with Monero”. Copy controls appear in the payment-link list; copy the updated HTML after changing the label. Optionally enable “Skip review and create invoice automatically” to open invoices directly. This is off by default; visits, including automated browsers, can consume invoice allowance and address capacity.

body.2: For the €20 reference, each purchase request calculates an XMR amount using the available informational quote. The invoice is defined in XMR and displays the quote source and timestamp. There is no rate lock or guaranteed EUR outcome. If the quote is unavailable, creation fails.
body.3: Need your own deployment first? Follow the <selfhost>self-hosting guide</selfhost>. A working view-only wallet and synchronized detection services are prerequisites.

embed.title: Copy your HTML button or reusable URL

body.1: Preview the branded button in the dashboard, then copy its HTML into a custom HTML block on your website. The graphic includes the xmrcheckout logo and links to the payment review page. No form, JavaScript, or merchant API key is needed in the snippet.
body.2: This example uses a reserved example domain and placeholder token. Copy your actual snippet from the dashboard; keep your wallet credentials and API key out of website HTML.
body.3: You can also copy the reusable URL and attach it to a normal link or your own website button. Both options show the product review page; the customer then submits a purchase request. With review enabled, opening a URL does not create an invoice. With automatic creation enabled, an active browser requests an invoice and opens it. The same tab resumes its current unpaid invoice; use “Start another purchase” for a separate order. Without JavaScript or browser storage, customers use the manual creation button.
body.4: Purchases use the saved receiving wallet, amount, confirmation target, and return URL. Editing HTML cannot override these settings.

invoices.title: Review each purchase in your invoice list

body.1: A successful submission opens an invoice with its own ID, XMR amount, payment instructions, and confirmation progress. Keep the invoice URL and use its ID when discussing a purchase with the customer.
body.2: Review payment-link invoices in Dashboard → Invoices. Search the product title or payment-link ID in invoice metadata. Each invoice retains a snapshot of the product settings; optional existing webhooks also include that metadata.
body.3: Payment detection and reaching your confirmation target are separate states. Review the invoice status before fulfilling an order. Payment links do not collect buyer details or host files. Use a <message>confirmation message</message> to show a download link or instructions after confirmation, or arrange delivery yourself using the invoice ID. A merchant return URL is navigation after confirmation.

confirmation-message.title: Show a confirmation message after payment

body.1: Each payment link can have its own Confirmation message. It appears on the buyer’s invoice page under “Message from the merchant” once the invoice reaches your required confirmations. Until then, the message is not sent to the browser: the page is rendered on the server and the public invoice status returns no message. Web addresses starting with http:// or https:// become clickable links.

3.1: Digital downloads. Selling five ebooks? Create five payment links, one per ebook, and put each ebook’s download link in that link’s message, for example “Thanks! Download your copy: https://your-site.example/files/ebook-1.pdf”.
3.2: Shared access details. A license key, course access code, or private group invitation that is the same for every buyer.
3.3: Delivery instructions. Next steps such as “Email your invoice ID to orders@your-site.example with your postal address” or “Book your session at https://your-site.example/book”.
3.4: Thank-you notes. A short note with links to support pages, documentation, or updates.

5.1: Every buyer of a link sees the same text, and a buyer can share it with others. For files you need to protect, host them where you control access, such as expiring or signed download links, or a store that checks the invoice ID. Use <webhooks>webhooks</webhooks> to issue unique keys or downloads per buyer.
5.2: The message follows your confirmation target. With zero confirmations it appears as soon as a payment is detected, before any block confirmation; choose at least one confirmation for content you cannot take back.
5.3: Each invoice keeps the message that was saved when it was created. Editing a link changes the message for new invoices only.
5.4: Messages are plain text up to 2,000 characters. Formatting and HTML are shown as typed. Files are not uploaded or hosted by XMR Checkout.
5.5: The message is merchant-provided information. XMR Checkout displays it but does not check its content or guarantee what it links to.

body.1: Open Edit settings on the link to change its product details or amount. Saved changes apply to future invoices, while existing invoices keep their original settings. The reusable URL and button continue to identify the same link.
body.2: Use Disable payment link to stop new purchases. Existing invoices remain valid and continue detection. Re-enable a link through its settings after correcting any unsupported saved currency or other invalid settings.

body.1: Creators, maintainers, and other recipients can use payment links to receive voluntary contributions directly to their own wallet. Each successful submission creates a separate invoice with payment detection and confirmation progress.

2.1: Create a payment link with a title such as “Support my project” and choose Customer enters the amount. Set Button text to Donate with Monero. Optionally set a minimum amount in XMR to avoid very small invoices.
2.2: Share the reusable URL on your profile or website, or copy the HTML button from the dashboard. You can attach the URL to your own “Support this project” button too.
2.3: Donors enter an amount and choose XMR or a supported fiat-reference currency on the review page, then create their invoice. To offer preset amounts instead, create a separate fixed-amount link for each.
2.4: Customer-entered links always show the review page. For fixed-amount links, keep the review step enabled if opening a shared URL should not create an invoice. Automatic creation is optional and consumes capacity when an active browser requests an invoice.

body.3: Each contribution is a separate payment initiated in the donor’s wallet. These links do not provide recurring collection or donor management. A supported fiat-reference amount is converted to an informational XMR amount at invoice creation; no rate or fiat outcome is guaranteed.
body.4: Example only: use the actual HTML or URL from your dashboard. Your credentials do not belong in the snippet. Donation links share the same <limits>invoice allowance, address capacity, and interrupted-submission limits</limits> as other payment links. Unpaid invoices consume capacity too.

body.1: People who hold Monero look for places that accept it. A copyable “Monero accepted here” badge and a printable sign are available in the dashboard.

2.1: Add a badge to your website. Open Dashboard → Payment links and copy the Monero accepted here badge into an HTML block. There is a dark badge for light backgrounds and a light badge for dark ones. The badge is a plain image with no tracking or account details.
2.2: Print a sign. Each payment link has a Printable sign with QR code. Customers scan it with their wallet to open the link. Use it at a counter, market stall, event table, or donation box. Signs show a price only for links fixed in XMR. For card-style checkout at a till, use a terminal and display the badge beside it.

1.1: The default public allowance is 10 successful invoice creations per merchant over a rolling 24 hours, shared across all payment links. The dashboard shows this deployment’s configured limit, usage, remaining allowance, and address availability. Refresh retrieves both snapshots; neither reserves capacity.
1.2: Other merchant invoice limits still apply. The address pool supports up to 199 invoice subaddresses per merchant, all within the default range every Monero wallet watches. Unpaid requests consume capacity too. An address can be reused after its prior invoices close and the default three-day cooldown passes. A fresh invoice does not guarantee a never-used address; a new late payment intended for an older invoice can still be confused with a newer one after reuse.
1.3: The default Nginx configuration also limits public purchase requests to 6 per minute per client IP, with burst 3. Operators can configure these limits and the reuse cooldown. Rate or capacity errors may include Retry-After guidance.
1.4: Plain HTML has no duplicate-submission recovery. Separate submissions can create separate invoices. If a response is interrupted, creation may already have succeeded. Do not automatically retry: check any invoice URL received or contact the merchant before submitting again.

body.2: A service outage can make checkout or status detection unavailable; payments already sent remain valid on-chain and you retain access to your wallet. A malicious visitor can consume your public allowance, so monitor usage and disable links when needed.
body.3: Developers can find the management endpoints and public form behavior in the <api>payment-link API reference</api>.

selfHost.metaTitle: How to Run a Self-Hosted Monero Checkout | XMR Checkout
selfHost.metaDescription: Set up XMR Checkout with Docker Compose, a view-only wallet, a Monero daemon, and reliable invoice detection.
selfHost.title: How to run a self-hosted Monero checkout.
selfHost.intro: This guide covers the deployment path for operators who want XMR Checkout running alongside infrastructure they control. It uses only a wallet address and private view key for payment detection.
selfHost.flowTitle: Customer to merchant wallet, with status reported by software.
selfHost.flowBody: Your store or dashboard creates an invoice. The hosted invoice page shows the amount, address, QR code, and wallet URI. A reconciler checks the configured wallet and Monero daemon for an incoming payment, then updates invoice status for your dashboard, API, and webhooks.
selfHost.createBody: Make an XMR invoice from the dashboard or API.
selfHost.observeBody: Watch the merchant wallet for the expected payment.
selfHost.reportBody: Read status through the UI, API, or webhooks.
selfHost.hostTitle: Gather the configuration before starting the stack.
selfHost.host1: A host that can run Docker Compose and persist Postgres and wallet data.
selfHost.host2: A public HTTPS site URL for hosted invoice pages and webhook destinations.
selfHost.host3: A Monero primary address and private view key. Never provide a private spend key.
selfHost.host4: A reachable Monero daemon and wallet-rpc target, either bundled or external.
selfHost.hostNote: The full environment variable reference and deployment notes are maintained in the repository README. Review them before exposing an installation to the public internet.
selfHost.composeRef: Read the Docker Compose deployment reference →
selfHost.dockerTitle: Start from the example environment and choose your node path.
selfHost.dockerBody: Copy the environment template, set the database and API values, configure the site URL, and add the view-only wallet settings. Then choose whether the reconciler should use a third-party daemon or a local daemon started by the Compose profile.
selfHost.dockerNote: A local daemon must finish syncing before payment detection is reliable. If you use the bundled wallet-rpc shards, keep their configured URL ordering stable because it determines shard ownership for view-only wallets.
selfHost.verifyTitle: Test one invoice before connecting a store.
selfHost.verify1: Open the dashboard and create a small test invoice in XMR.
selfHost.verify2: Open the hosted invoice page and confirm that its address, amount, QR code, and expiry are visible.
selfHost.verify3: Send the test payment from a wallet you control and wait for the configured confirmation target.
selfHost.verify4: Confirm that the dashboard and public invoice page show the observed status before adding webhooks or order automation.
selfHost.troubleTitle: Check the observation path in order.
selfHost.troubleBody: If an invoice remains at zero confirmations, check wallet-rpc reachability, daemon connectivity, current daemon height, and the time of the last successful reconcile. Inspect the API, reconciler, wallet-rpc, and daemon logs before changing wallet configuration.
selfHost.troubleNote: The service only observes payments. If the UI or reconciler is unavailable, a valid on-chain payment still goes from the customer to your wallet; status updates may be delayed until the service is available again.
selfHost.continueApi: Continue to API and webhook integration →

api.metaTitleShort: Integrating the Monero Payment API and Webhooks
api.metaTitle: Integrating the Monero Payment API and Webhooks | XMR Checkout
api.metaDescription: Connect a store to XMR Checkout with invoice creation, hosted payment pages, public status checks, and webhook events.
api.webhooksBody: Register a public HTTPS endpoint through the dashboard or the API, then select the events you want to receive. Native events include invoice.created, invoice.partially_paid, invoice.payment_detected, invoice.confirmed, and invoice.expired.
api.verifyBody: Compare the X-Webhook-Secret header with the secret stored by your server before processing the JSON payload.
api.title: Integrating the Monero payment API and webhooks.
api.intro: Connect an existing order flow to invoice creation, the hosted payment page, public status checks, and webhook events without exposing credentials in browser code.
api.flowTitle: Create, redirect, observe, and update your order.
api.createBody: Call the authenticated invoice endpoint with an XMR amount and your order metadata.
api.sendCustomerBody: Use the returned invoice URL for the hosted payment page.
api.observeBody: Poll the public invoice endpoint or receive the relevant webhook event.
api.updateBody: Use invoice.confirmed as the confirmation signal for your own order flow.
api.createTitle: Keep the API call on your server.
api.createText: Authenticated endpoints use an API key. Send the amount in XMR, choose a confirmation target when needed, and include an internal order reference in metadata so your webhook handler can connect an event to your order.
api.createNote: The response contains the invoice id, payment details, and hosted invoice URL. Store the invoice id with your order and redirect the customer to that URL.
api.statusTitle: Use the public invoice endpoint for a simple fallback.
api.statusBody: The public endpoint does not need an API key and returns the invoice status and payment details. Use it for customer-facing refreshes or as a polling fallback while your server waits for a webhook.
api.statusNote: Treat the confirmation target as part of your order policy. A detected payment and a confirmed invoice are different states; your order flow should use the state that matches what you need.
api.webhooksTitle: Subscribe to the events your server needs.
api.ackBody: Return a successful HTTP response only after your handler has safely recorded the event for its own processing.
api.redeliver: Failed deliveries are recorded in webhook history and can be redelivered from the API. Make your handler safe to run more than once by keying order updates on the invoice id and event state.
api.securityTitle: Separate customer-facing pages from server credentials.
api.security1: Keep API keys and webhook secrets in server-side environment variables. Do not ship them in browser JavaScript.
api.security2: Use HTTPS for webhook destinations and validate the secret before acting on an event.
api.security3: Your integration observes invoice status; it does not request spend authority or move funds.
